hook_text: Your map says 6,5. Six point five what? Here is the three-step habit that turns a ruler reading into a real distance.
clip_script: A map is the real world shrunk to fit on paper, and the scale tells you how much it shrank. Say the scale is one centimetre represents two kilometres. The school and the clinic measure six and a half centimetres apart. Six and a half times two: thirteen kilometres. Measure, multiply, say the unit. Now the trap. The road between them bends. A ruler only measures the straight line, the way a bird would fly. So lay a piece of string along the road, follow every curve, straighten it and measure again. That is how far the taxi actually drives. One more trap: if the map was enlarged on a photocopier, the words "one centimetre represents two kilometres" are now wrong, but the little line scale printed on the map grew with it, so it is still right. Measure, multiply, say the unit, and trust the line scale.
visual_style: A whiteboard street map with a school and a clinic, a ruler sliding between them, the numbers 6,5 times 2 equals 13 km appearing; then a string tracing a bendy road and being pulled straight against the ruler.
mood: Practical, confident, a little bit of a magic trick.
pacing: Quick setup, a clean calculation, then two traps revealed one after the other.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and get every map distance right this term.
